enrichment.short_title: Manchester armed robbery conspiracy conviction appeals
key_facts: Hamlett, Beddow, McCartney and Hulme were convicted after a seven-week trial of conspiracy to rob in relation to about twenty armed robberies or attempted robberies in the Manchester area between 1996 and 1998.
The Crown case rested heavily on accomplice evidence from Raymond Lally, who admitted involvement in most offences and implicated co-defendants; some defendants were acquitted.
Conviction appeals challenged Lally's credibility, late and non-disclosure, summing-up on adverse inference and identification, and alleged jury discharge failures.
On sentence, Hulme received 22 years; Hamlett 19 years; McCartney 11 years consecutive to an existing eight-year term; Beddow 17 years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals against conviction and sentence following convictions for conspiracy to rob in the Crown Court.
enrichment.outcome: Conviction appeals dismissed; Hulme's sentence appeal dismissed; all appellants' sentences reduced by twelve months for breach of Article 6(1) delay.
enrichment.ratio: Convictions based on accomplice evidence are safe where the jury was properly directed to look for independent support and the trial judge's handling of disclosure, identification and adverse inference did not render the trial unfair; long custodial terms for career armed robbers carrying firearms are not manifestly excessive, but delay in hearing an appeal may justify a modest sentence reduction under Article 6(1).
legal_issues: Safety of convictions founded on uncorroborated accomplice evidence
Material non-disclosure and late disclosure
Directions on adverse inference and identification
Whether the jury should have been discharged
Appropriate length of sentence for multiple armed bank robberies
Remedy for delay in hearing criminal appeals

linked_authorities.name: Condron and Another v United Kingdom

confidence.notes: Long judgment with explicit disposal on conviction safety, sentence appeals and Article 6 reduction.

enrichment.short_title: Care proceedings used to resist immigration removal
key_facts: Care proceedings were brought for two children after the father, facing removal following failed asylum claims, made threats of suicide and harm to the family on the eve of deportation.
The local authority later concluded, supported by a clinical psychologist's report, that neither parent posed a continuing risk and that the proceedings should end.
The parents sought to continue interim care orders to resist removal to their country of origin, relying on conditions abroad and the brother's immigration status.
The Secretary of State was joined as a party; removal powers could not be overridden by a Children Act order.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court care proceedings transferred from the county court to determine whether interim care orders and the proceedings should continue.
enrichment.outcome: Interim care orders discharged and care proceedings dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Where care proceedings concerning children liable to removal raise no genuine child-protection dispute apart from immigration, the court must exercise Part IV jurisdiction sparingly and must not allow its process to be used to influence immigration decisions; without reasonable grounds for believing significant harm attributable to parental care, continuation of proceedings confers no welfare advantage and may amount to abuse of process.
legal_issues: Overlap between Children Act proceedings and immigration removal
Section 31(2) threshold and section 38(2) interim care orders
Whether risk on return to the country of origin can justify care proceedings
Abuse of process where proceedings are used to frustrate removal
Relationship between family court welfare assessment and Secretary of State's Article 8 balancing exercise

linked_authorities.name: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex p T
R v Secretary of State for Home Department ex p Gangadeen
London Borough of Southwark v B

confidence.notes: Full judgment with detailed exposition of immigration/family law interface and clear order discharging proceedings.

enrichment.short_title: Wet or icy pathway causation in slip claim
key_facts: Mrs Pigford, a home help, slipped on brick block paving on a City of Sunderland housing estate walkway in December 1998.
The council conceded liability if the surface was wet because of its known slipperiness when wet, but not if ice was present because gritting was not required.

The recorder found on balance of probabilities that the fall was caused by wet, slippery blockwork rather than ice, relying on Mrs Pigford's trial evidence and neighbour Mrs Harrison's evidence despite earlier documents saying she slipped on ice.
The council appealed on the ground that the finding was perverse.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a county court recorder's finding of fact on causation in a personal injury claim.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed by majority (Sedley and Rix LJJ; Aldous LJ dissenting).
enrichment.ratio: An appellate court will not overturn a trial judge's finding on whether a claimant slipped on wet or icy paving as perverse where there was evidence supporting the finding, the judge accepted a truthful witness's account, and meteorological evidence was consistent with thaw conditions; inconsistent prior statements do not automatically make the judge's conclusion impossible.
legal_issues: Whether the recorder's causation finding was perverse
Weight to be given to contemporaneous accident reports stating ice
Burden of proof on causation in occupiers' liability claims
Appellate intervention in fact-finding

confidence.notes: Judgment centres on a discrete factual issue with clear majority and dissent on appeal outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Section 65 appeal rights and section 73 certification
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Duka, Kosovan asylum claimants facing removal, sought to rely on Article 8 family life with Mrs Duka's brother Renols Kabashi, who had been granted leave on medical grounds after a successful appeal.
Pitchford J had earlier rejected their human rights challenge; further representations and a psychiatric report did not materially change the position.
The Secretary of State refused to treat further representations as a fresh claim, issued removal directions, and later certified under section 73(8) to block a section 65 appeal.
The claimants argued the December 2002 refusal letter and removal directions were appealable decisions and that the section 73(8) certificate was invalid.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of immigration removal and certification under section 73(8) of the Immigration and Asylum Act 1999.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; relief refused because the claim lacked merit and a section 73(2) certificate would have been issued.
enrichment.ratio: A refusal of further representations that confirms an applicant has no basis of stay and will be removed is a section 65 appealable decision under the Immigration Acts; section 73(8) certification cannot preclude an appeal already validly pending, but where the underlying human rights claim could reasonably have been raised earlier and has no real prospect of success, the court may refuse relief even if the certificate is unlawful.
legal_issues: Whether a refusal of further representations attracts a section 65 appeal
Validity of section 73(8) certification after an appeal is lodged
Distinction between section 73(2) and section 73(8) certification
Article 8 proportionality where a dependent sibling has leave on medical grounds
Discretion to refuse relief where claim lacks merit

linked_authorities.name: R (Kariharan & Koneswaran) v Secretary of State

confidence.notes: Detailed statutory construction and clear disposal, though some certification law was transitional under the 1999 Act.

enrichment.short_title: CFA success fee and ATE premium on slip claim
key_facts: Mrs Abrew slipped on dried spaghetti in a Tesco aisle in August 2000 and settled her personal injury claim for £3,500 after liability was accepted.
Her solicitors acted under a CFA with a 100% success fee and took ATE insurance with a £790 premium for £100,000 cover.
Detailed assessment reduced total costs from £8,882 to £4,862.47; the defendants appealed the insurance premium, success fee and costs of assessment.
The appeal was heard by Lord Justice Latham as a rehearing on costs officer Worthy's assessment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on costs only following Part 8 proceedings after detailed assessment of a CFA-funded slipping claim.
enrichment.outcome: Insurance premium reduced to £400; success fee of 50% upheld; costs of detailed assessment unchanged; defendants' appeal largely dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: In assessing ATE premiums and CFA success fees at the time they were fixed in 2000, before later Callery v Gray guidance, a court may allow a modestly higher premium and a 50% success fee where the slipping claim carried some litigation risk, but excessive cover and premium levels may be reduced; proportionality objections to detailed assessment costs may fail where the paying party broadly challenged the bill.
legal_issues: Reasonableness of ATE insurance premium level and cover
Appropriate CFA success fee for a supermarket slip claim
Retrospective application of later costs authorities
Proportionality of costs of detailed assessment under CPR 47.18

confidence.notes: Clear costs ruling on three distinct heads with explicit figures.

enrichment.short_title: HFEA power to license embryo tissue typing
key_facts: Mr and Mrs Hashmi sought IVF with pre-implantation genetic diagnosis so that an embryo could be selected for tissue compatibility with their son Zain, who had beta thalassaemia major and needed a stem-cell transplant.
The Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority announced in December 2001 that tissue typing to select a compatible embryo could be licensed in principle, subject to conditions.
Quintavalle challenged the decision by judicial review; Maurice Kay J quashed it as outside the Authority's statutory powers.
The Authority appealed, arguing tissue typing was a licensable treatment service to determine embryo suitability for implantation.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a judicial review quashing the HFEA's decision in principle to allow licensed embryo tissue typing.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the judge's quashing order was set aside and the claim for judicial review refused.
enrichment.ratio: Tissue typing of embryos for compatibility with an affected sibling falls within the Human Fertilisation and Embryology Act 1990 as a practice designed to determine whether an embryo is suitable to be placed in a woman, because suitability may be judged by reference to the family's established medical needs and the HFEA may license PGD and related biopsy services subject to conditions.
legal_issues: Whether tissue typing uses an embryo within the meaning of the 1990 Act
Whether PGD for tissue compatibility is a licensable treatment service
Construction of Schedule 2 paragraph 1(1)(d) suitability for implantation
Extent of HFEA discretion to authorise saviour-sibling selection

linked_authorities.name: Quintavalle v Human Fertilisation and Embryology Authority

confidence.notes: Leading early authority on HFEA licensing of tissue typing with detailed statutory analysis and clear appeal outcome.

enrichment.short_title: Automatic incorporation of NJC pay awards

statutes_considered.title: Transfer of Undertakings (Protection of Employment) Regulations 1981

key_facts: After a TUPE transfer from Southend Borough Council to Glendale Managed Services, fourteen employees including Mr Graham did not receive NJC pay increases of 3% from April 2000 and 3.5% from April 2001.
Their written particulars stated pay would normally be in accordance with NJC terms as adopted by the authority from time to time.
Evidence showed the council had historically paid NJC rises without formal resolutions or individual notification.
Employment tribunals held the increases were contractually due; the EAT refused a full appeal hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Employer's appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal refusal to grant a full hearing on unlawful deduction from wages.
enrichment.ratio: Where employment particulars provide that pay will normally follow NJC terms as adopted from time to time, nationally agreed pay rises are incorporated without a fresh formal approval each year unless the employer positively decides to depart from the norm and gives the employee notice of that departure; past conduct may inform the meaning of the contractual term.
legal_issues: Construction of 'normally' and 'as adopted by the authority from time to time'
Whether NJC pay awards require express annual adoption
Admissibility of subsequent conduct in interpreting employment contracts
Implied duty to notify employees before departing from normal pay terms

linked_authorities.name: System Floors UK Ltd v Daniel
Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich Building Society

confidence.notes: Focused contractual construction issue with unanimous Court of Appeal reasoning.

enrichment.short_title: Article 6 and race claim by serving soldier

statutes_considered.title: Race Relations (Complaints to Industrial Tribunals) (Armed Forces) Regulations 1997

key_facts: Mr Mangera, a serving soldier for over ten years, alleged race discrimination because halal meat was not provided in his rations for most of his service and he had to pay for food he could not eat.
Race Relations Act complaints by service personnel must generally be preceded by use of service redress procedures.
Mr Mangera had not made the required complaint before presenting his Employment Tribunal claim.
He argued Article 6 entitled him to bypass the precondition and that Pellegrin v France did not exclude discrimination claims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary appeal on whether Article 6 applies to a Race Relations Act employment claim brought by a serving soldier.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; permission to appeal to the House of Lords refused.
enrichment.ratio: Under Pellegrin v France, Article 6 does not apply to disputes between administrative authorities and public servants, including armed forces personnel, relating to conditions of service; a Race Relations Act claim about rations is an employment dispute enforceable only through the Employment Tribunal and cannot be recharacterised as a tort claim to avoid the exclusion.
legal_issues: Application of Pellegrin v France to armed forces personnel
Whether a race discrimination claim is an employment dispute or tort claim
Whether service redress preconditions infringe Article 6 right of access to court
Application of Article 14 if Article 6 is excluded

confidence.notes: Preliminary issue decided on established Pellegrin jurisprudence with clear appeal dismissal.

enrichment.short_title: Refusal to set aside default possession order
key_facts: Sterling Credit Ltd obtained a default possession order against Miss Abrahams' Cornwall property after mortgage proceedings.
Miss Abrahams applied to set aside the order under CPR 39.3, alleging the legal charge was forged by a cohabitee.
The deputy district judge heard oral evidence, disbelieved Miss Abrahams on promptness, good reason for non-attendance and merits, and dismissed the application.
His Honour Judge Vincent upheld that decision on review; Miss Abrahams sought second-tier permission to appeal out of time.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Renewed application for permission to appeal out of time against refusal to set aside a default possession order.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A second-tier appeal under CPR 52.13 requires an important point of principle or other compelling reason; a judge's adverse credibility finding after hearing oral evidence on a CPR 39.3 application will not be reopened merely because the defendant was effectively labelled dishonest, and the appellate court is not in as good a position as the trial judge on credibility.
legal_issues: Requirements under CPR 39.3(5) to set aside judgment after non-attendance
Scope of second-tier appeal under CPR 52.13
Whether a finding of dishonesty constitutes a compelling reason to appeal
Appellate review of credibility findings on interlocutory applications

confidence.notes: Short procedural judgment with explicit refusal of permission and clear fact findings below.

enrichment.short_title: Ultra vires hospital order after unfitness finding

statutes_considered.title: Criminal Procedure (Insanity and Unfitness to Plead) Act 1991

key_facts: The applicant was charged with burglary; a jury found him unfit to plead, and a second jury found under section 4A that he did the act alleged.
The Crown Court made section 37 and section 41 Mental Health Act orders although there had been no conviction.
Earlier appeal against sentence had been refused because no conviction existed; the ultra vires nature of the disposal had not then been raised.
The applicant sought remission for trial via schedule 1 paragraph 4 but the defective hospital order blocked that route.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Divisional Court judicial review to quash ultra vires Mental Health Act orders made after unfitness and actus reus findings.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; section 37 and section 41 orders set aside; matter remitted to the Crown Court for proper section 5 disposal.
enrichment.ratio: Where a defendant is found unfit to plead and to have done the act charged, disposal must be by admission order under section 5(2) of the Criminal Procedure (Insanity) Act 1964 and not by section 37 or section 41 Mental Health Act orders, which require conviction; an appeal against disposal after unfitness proceedings lies to the Divisional Court rather than as a sentence appeal under the Criminal Appeal Act 1968.
legal_issues: Correct disposal after section 4A finding that the accused did the act
Whether section 37 and section 41 orders can be made without conviction
Route of challenge to disposal orders following unfitness proceedings
Effect of schedule 1 paragraph 4 remission power

confidence.notes: Clear statutory analysis with explicit quashing of orders and remittal.
